summary:
Earth Jukebox is a web app that turns NASA Earth Information Center visualizations into music, generated live from the video frames. You pick a "record" (lightning seen from the ISS, aerosols, ocean currents, night lights or global CO2) and the real NASA video plays while our app reads every frame, decodes its colours with NASA's own legends, and turns what it finds into sound: where lightning strikes, which particles fill the air, how warm the ocean is.

The challenge asked us to translate sight into sound so blind and low-vision people can reach NASA's Earth science. Earth Jukebox does that with real NASA data, sound that carries information you can test by ear in our built-in Ear Test, and an interface fully usable by keyboard and screen reader.

It matters because our changing planet should be understandable by everyone, not only those who can see a heatmap.
details:
What it does

Earth Jukebox is a jukebox of NASA Earth visualizations. Each one is a “record”. Choose one and the real NASA video plays while the app listens to it frame by frame and turns it into music in real time. Nothing is pre-recorded: pause the video and the sound stops; skip ahead and the music follows.

There are three ways to listen. Play runs the record. Explore lets you pause and move a cursor with the mouse or arrow keys to hear the value under it. Ear Test plays two short clips, one in each ear, and asks which has more — for example, which has more lightning — proof that the sound carries real information, not just mood.

How it works

  1. Frame: about 30 times a second, each video frame is copied onto a small hidden canvas (about 160 × 90 pixels). Legends and date stamps are masked out.
  2. Legend decode: the app reads the pixels and matches their colours to NASA’s own colour legends. It also compares each frame with the last to find what just appeared, and groups nearby points into clusters.
  3. Music rules: each record has its own rules that turn those facts into sound. Notes snap to a pentatonic scale so nothing clashes; events are gathered onto a steady beat; at most a few notes play at once so it never becomes noise. On flat maps, north sounds higher and west sits in your left ear.
  4. Output: a Tone.js audio engine plays the instruments through a limiter. At the same time, ripples appear on the video where each note came from, captions describe every sound, and a screen-reader live region announces what is happening.

Everything runs in the browser. There is no server, so it is fast, private, and keeps working offline once loaded.

The five records, and why each sounds the way it does

  • Lightning (ISS, 2017–2023) is rhythm. Each new flash is a soft mallet note: north is high, west is left, bigger storms are louder, and a hum swells with total lightning. Lightning is sudden, so it should be heard as a beat — and you can hear storm season migrate north and south across the year.
  • Aerosols (GEOS, Aug–Sep 2024) is an orchestra. Smoke is a low brass, dust a breathy wind, sea salt soft bells, sulfate plucked notes. Ears separate instruments the way they pick out a violin in an orchestra, so each particle gets its own voice. Solo the dust and you hear the Sahara drift west across the Atlantic.
  • Ocean currents is a texture. NASA’s colour legend is decoded back into temperature: warmer water plays higher, swirling currents sparkle, and a scanner beam sweeps west to east so you hear the ocean one slice at a time.
  • Night lights (2012–2023) is change. A chord fills out as the world brightens; on the change map, new lights ring a rising bell and lights going out fall as a low tone. Rising and falling map onto growth and loss without any training.
  • Carbon dioxide (DYAMOND, early 2020) is a drone. A fixed reference tone holds steady while a second drone rises, brightens and grows louder as more high-CO₂ colour fills the view, with a wobble for day and night. The camera orbits the globe, so this record deliberately ignores screen position rather than invent geography.

The story: why it should move you

We wanted the sound to carry feeling as well as facts. The CO₂ record is built around a gap: a calm reference tone, and a second voice that keeps pulling away from it. You don’t need a chart to feel the tension — it is the sound of a planet drifting from where it was. Night lights let you hear human life spread and, in places, go dark. And the aerosols record shows how connected Earth is: dust from a desert crossing an entire ocean, audible as one instrument moving from one ear to the other. Our aim was music pleasant enough to listen to for minutes, honest enough to learn from, and urgent enough to remember.

Accessibility

Every feature works by keyboard. Screen readers announce the track, date and values through a live region. H reads the on-screen readouts aloud, F describes the current frame in words, and L explains what each sound means. Every sound has a visible caption for deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and a spectrum ring keeps showing the music even when muted. There is a high-contrast mode, reduced-motion support, and an automated test that checks colour contrast against WCAG AA.

Benefits

Blind and low-vision people can explore NASA Earth science on their own terms. Sighted people get a second way to notice patterns their eyes skim past. Teachers and museums, including the Earth Information Center, get a multi-sensory way to present climate data. And the design is extensible: a new visualization needs one config file and one rules file; the engine, instruments and accessibility layer are shared.

What we hope to achieve

We hope Earth Jukebox shows that NASA’s visualizations can be heard as clearly as they are seen — and that sonification can be accurate, musical and accessible at the same time. Next we want to add more EIC records, a built-in voice guide, haptic feedback on phones, and audio export for classrooms.

Honest limits

The sound follows the visualization, not the raw sensor data. Ocean temperature is estimated from NASA’s colour legend. CO₂ follows the amount of high-CO₂ colour on screen, not exact parts per million. NASA’s lightning date file lists 2003 where it means 2023; we keep the file unedited, show the corrected year, and document it.

How it is creative

Most sonifications map one number to pitch. Earth Jukebox gives every dataset its own musical identity, chosen to match what the data is: lightning is rhythm, aerosols are an orchestra with one instrument per particle, the ocean is a flowing texture with a scanning melody, night lights are rising and falling tones, and CO2 is a drone pulling away from a fixed reference. The music is generated live from NASA's frames, so it can never drift out of sync with the picture, and the Ear Test turns the whole thing into a game that proves the sound carries information.

Factors our team considered

Accuracy: we use NASA's own colour legends and say openly where values are estimated. Honest geography: position is only used where the map is flat, never on the orbiting CO2 globe. Listening comfort: all notes sit on a pentatonic scale so nothing clashes, mostly between about 65 Hz and 2 kHz, below the range where hearing is most sensitive, with a limiter so it never gets too loud. Accessibility: keyboard-only control, screen-reader announcements, captions for every sound, high contrast and reduced motion. Reliability: everything runs in the browser with no server, so it works offline and keeps user data private.

Tools and languages

TypeScript, React, Vite, Tone.js (Web Audio), Zustand, Motion, the HTML Canvas API with requestVideoFrameCallback, Vitest for unit tests (analysis and mapping tested with synthetic frames), oxlint, ffmpeg for preparing the videos, Vercel for hosting, and GitHub. No special hardware: it runs in any modern browser.
